descriptions: that from which the origin, sustenance and dissolution of this world proceed (BS 1.1.2)
known from scripture (BS 1.1.3), the purport of all Upaniṣadic texts (BS 1.1.4)
material and efficient cause of the world (BS 1.4.23)
the goal attained by the liberated, from which there is no return (BS 4.4.22)
negations: the 'not so, not so' denies 'so much' (the two forms) of Brahman (BS 3.2.22)
relation_to_self: Debated within the sūtras themselves: Āśmarathya, Auḍulomi and Kāśakṛtsna give three accounts (BS 1.4.20–22); every Vedānta school reads the sūtras on this point differently.
relation_to_world: Brahman is the world's cause; the effect is non-different from the cause (BS 2.1.14); the manner (real or apparent transformation) is the chief point of divergence among commentators.
caveat: This view records what the sūtras state on their face. Each Vedānta school's reading (Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, Bhedābheda etc.) is its own view, and the schools deny that the others' readings are the sūtras' meaning.

names.name: Sākṣin (as witness of the three states)
Īśvara (Brahman as associated with māyā, empirical level)

descriptions: existence, consciousness, infinitude — satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma (TU 2.1.1) as its own-nature definition (svarūpa-lakṣaṇa)
one without a second (ekam evādvitīyam, ChU 6.2.1)
the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) of the world-appearance, as the rope is of the snake
the world's cause, defined incidentally (taṭastha-lakṣaṇa) as that from which the world arises (BS 1.1.2)
negations: neti neti — not so, not so (BĀU 2.3.6; BS 3.2.22)
no dissolution, no origination, none bound, no seeker, no liberated — this is the highest truth (GK 2.32)
without parts, attributes, action or difference of any of the three kinds (sajātīya, vijātīya, svagata)
relation_to_self: Identical: the inner self (pratyag-ātman) of every being is Brahman (tat tvam asi; ahaṃ brahmāsmi). The jīva is Brahman appearing as limited or reflected through adjuncts produced by ignorance.
relation_to_world: The world is superimposed on Brahman and is its apparent transformation (vivarta); Brahman is its material and efficient cause through māyā. The world is real for empirical purposes (vyāvahārika) until knowledge, then sublated; ultimately it is not other than Brahman.
caveat: Advaita accepts that truth is one (and reads RV 1.164.46 in that sense), but the one is non-dual consciousness without any internal difference: the personal Lord is Brahman as associated with māyā, real at the empirical level only. Advaita would reject any 'one-truth' reading that makes the world, or plural selves, or a personal God ultimately real, and rejects equating its Brahman with a sum or organism of parts.

descriptions: pure consciousness, the locus and object of the one beginningless ignorance
the prototype (bimba) of which the jīva is the reflection
relation_to_self: The jīva is Brahman's reflection (pratibimba) in avidyā/the inner organ; the reflection is not unreal but identical with the prototype, as a face in a mirror is the face itself.
relation_to_world: The world is the transformation (pariṇāma) of avidyā and the apparent transformation (vivarta) of Brahman, which is the locus of avidyā.
caveat: Shares Advaita's ultimate; differs from the Bhāmatī line only in the explanatory theory of how the one appears as many. Partisans of the Vivaraṇa hold their theory to be the correct one, not merely a method.

descriptions: immeasurable bliss and knowledge, deathless, whose apparent transformations the elements are, through two indescribable ignorances (Bhāmatī, opening verse)
relation_to_self: The jīva is Brahman as delimited (avacchinna) by the inner organ; ignorance resides in the jīvas, not in pure Brahman.
relation_to_world: The world is Brahman's apparent transformation (vivarta) through the avidyās of the jīvas, with Brahman as its object.
caveat: Shares Advaita's ultimate; differs only in the theory of the locus of ignorance and of the jīva. Partisans hold this theory to be correct.
